WEIGHT-SPACE PROGRAMMING · CONTROL PILOT

Astra weight programming from random initialization

Five control environments, prospective forecasts, feedback ablations, and policy observability.

Updated November 9, 2026 · seed-7 pilots · 100-episode comparisons and 20-episode mechanism tests

New: HalfCheetah and Humanoid · What Astra changed · Feedback ablation · Original Astra vs SAC pilot · Next experiments

New tasks: HalfCheetah and Humanoid

Completed result. SAC clearly leads on HalfCheetah: mean return 3,468 versus Astra's 686. On Humanoid, Astra scores 544 versus SAC's 486, but both fall well before the 1,000-step limit. The small Humanoid advantage is not evidence of reliable humanoid locomotion.

This first scaling pass uses one fresh full-feedback gpt-6-astra invocation and one CleanRL SAC run per environment, starting from identical seed-7 random actor tensors. Each method receives 36,864 online interactions. SAC trained on the two workstation GPUs; Astra submitted eight numerical policies and committed candidate 8. The comparison uses 100 shared held-out resets, 61000–61099, with deterministic actions.

Training curves and forecasts made before feedback

The top plots show SAC's exploratory training episodes and a trailing 10-episode mean. The bottom plots show Astra's deterministic candidate feedback, its point forecasts, and its stated 80% uncertainty intervals. These are different measurement protocols, not matched held-out learning curves.

Before every submission, Astra predicted the next feedback block's mean return, mean completed episode length, and mean observed root x velocity. The parent recorded and hashed those forecasts before simulation. Each block contains 4,096 transitions. Forecast velocity uses the next-observation root coordinate, which differs from the center-of-mass velocity used for Humanoid forward reward.

Do the forecasts beat a simple reference?

The persistence reference predicts that the next block will equal the previous observed block. Lower mean absolute error is better. The table scores each task's seven distinct candidate policies; candidate 8 repeats candidate 7 and is excluded here because its feedback score was already observed. All eight submissions remain visible in the curves.

Return forecasts do not beat persistence on either task. High interval coverage comes with broad intervals. HalfCheetah episode-length predictions are trivial under its fixed time limit. Velocity prediction results are mixed. Seven adaptive forecasts per task are too few to establish reliable calibration or a general predictive advantage.

These are aggregate policy-outcome predictions, not next-state or multi-step dynamics forecasts. They therefore do not establish an internal physics world model. Unlike retrospective explanations, they do give a recorded, prospective prediction signal that can be tested more rigorously in future runs.

Protocol and scope

Editors received full trajectories, initial random weights, architecture, action bounds, and observation/action meanings. No trained policies, prior experiment results, simulator source, XML, or separate physics-parameter files were supplied. Native Humanoid observations themselves include inertia and force features. Each editor had a fresh context and no access to the other task.

The native v4 environments are retained for consistency: HalfCheetah has 17 observations and 6 actions; Humanoid has 376 observations and 17 actions. Do not combine these scores with v5 results as if the environments were identical. Forecast commitments are an additional prompt requirement in these runs, so this is not a perfectly identical replication of the earlier three-task protocol.

Both editors and both SAC runs completed. All final evaluations began after the editors committed; test results did not influence policy selection. Reduced-feedback arms and additional initialization seeds have not yet been run on these two environments.

What is Astra doing? A Walker2d seed-7 case study

Observable finding. Astra constructs a compact controller from physics/control priors, then revises signs and gains using experience and adds a small amount of new control logic. These artifacts cannot establish whether Astra uses an internal physics world model. Controller tuning, use of experience, and internal predictive reasoning are not mutually exclusive.

We traced the completed full-feedback Walker2d editor from the ablation below: its numerical submissions, construction code, recorded pre-evaluation rationales, and development trajectories. Initialization seed 7 sets the random policy weights. The example rollout uses environment reset seed 52000; these are different kinds of seeds.

A compact controller inside the neural network

The actor has 73,484 parameter slots, but its final policy has only 142 nonzero entries. We recovered an exact compact control law with 38 nonzero coefficients. Many are tied by symmetry, so this is not a count of independent degrees of freedom.

action = tanh(K @ observation + H @ relu(observation) + b)

The affine matrix K has 32 nonzero coefficients, H has two velocity-dependent ReLU terms, and b has four nonzero biases. This is algebraic recovery from a verified network topology, without regression or fitting. The maximum action discrepancy on 2,304 common development states is 1.58 × 10⁻⁷, from floating-point evaluation order.

For example, the right-knee command before tanh is:

u = -3 * knee_angle - 0.04 * knee_angular_velocity
    - 0.15 - 0.09 * max(hip_angular_velocity, 0)

The deployed policy is a reactive control law with no recurrent state, transition-prediction module, or imagined rollout module. That describes the policy artifact, not the editor's internal computation while designing it.

The eight submissions

Candidate 1 replaces every initial actor coordinate. Later revisions change only 8–28 stored coordinates at a time. The following descriptions summarize recorded submission rationales and verified code changes; they are not access to hidden model reasoning.

CandidateObservable changeCoordinates changed vs previousDevelopment return
1Construct a joint-PD controller from prior knowledge73,4841.79
2Reverse torso-feedback signs and remove hip bias18411.57
3Reduce derivative gains after reported chatter28326.78
4Add ankle balance and forward-speed feedback8652.89
5Strengthen existing ankle balance gains81,008.11
6Add differential hip excitation and two knee-flexion terms161,209.36
7Increase gait excitation and clearance18855.48
8Revert exactly to candidate 6181,209.36

Candidate 3 tests a specific diagnosis: lower derivative gains to suppress rapid torque oscillation. Average step-to-step action change falls from 0.798 to 0.002, and action saturation falls from 21.9% to 0%. Return initially falls too: reducing chatter addresses one failure mode but does not solve balance. These action-change measurements exclude jumps across episode resets.

Do the added components actually help?

After commitment, we evaluated component removals on 20 fresh shared reset seeds, 52000–52019. These diagnostics were never returned to Astra and did not change policy selection. Removing added ankle balance subtracts the candidate-3-to-5 ankle changes while retaining the final hip and knee additions. Other removals hold the remaining final controller fixed.

ControllerMean returnHorizon survivalMean speed (m/s)Return change vs final [95% CI]
Final controller1,211.39100%0.212+0.00 [0.00, 0.00]
Remove all candidate-6 additions1,008.35100%0.008-203.04 [-203.89, -202.22]
Remove added ankle balance356.740%0.559-854.66 [-864.06, -844.24]
Remove hip excitation and biases1,008.38100%0.008-203.01 [-203.86, -202.20]
Remove knee-flexion terms1,008.05100%0.008-203.35 [-204.19, -202.52]
Remove ankle speed braking506.480%0.519-704.92 [-763.15, -640.83]

Paired bootstrap intervals describe reset-episode variation conditional on this one policy construction, not variation across editor calls. Components interact; these differences are not an additive attribution of reward. Survival means reaching the 1,000-step horizon.

Removing added ankle balance or speed braking produces faster motion followed by failure. Removing either hip excitation or the two knee-flexion terms restores near-standing behavior. Their combination supports modest forward movement. This demonstrates functional contributions in this policy without identifying how Astra represented the physics.

The final mean return decomposes into 1,000.00 survival reward + 211.64 forward reward − 0.24 control cost = 1,211.39. About 83% comes from survival. The decomposition was checked against every simulator reward in these episodes; control cost is not physical energy use.

Metrics now recorded

  • Parameter changes by tensor; nonzero coordinates; compact-controller coefficients and new terms.
  • Action differences on a fixed common state pool, saturation, step-to-step variation, and torso-angle RMS.
  • Episode survival, forward speed, displacement, and separate survival/progress/control-cost rewards.
  • Paired component-removal outcomes, per-episode records, and a complete time series for reset 52000.

What remains unknown about an internal world model?

No prospective numerical dynamics or outcome predictions were recorded from Astra. World-model prediction accuracy is unavailable, not zero. A compact final policy neither proves nor disproves an internal world model in the editor. Submitted explanations also do not provide reliable access to its internal computation.

A discriminating next experiment would require Astra to commit numerical next-state, return, speed, and survival predictions with uncertainty before feedback. We would score prediction error and calibration, test transfer under hidden dynamics changes, and compare real with absent or shuffled feedback. Predictions need parent-side recording before evaluation; retrospective explanations cannot substitute for these measurements.

Scope: 11 unique policies × 20 resets = 220 new diagnostic episodes and 120,327 simulator transitions. Candidate 8 repeats candidate 6, whose evaluation is reused. This is post-hoc analysis of one completed editor, with no new Astra invocation or feedback. It is not a new pre-registered benchmark or a general claim about internal representations.

Feedback ablation: how much experience does Astra need?

Ablation result. Without environment feedback, Astra still constructs a successful Pendulum controller, but its Hopper and Walker2d policies fail quickly. Walker2d shows the clearest separation between feedback types: full trajectories score 1,210, returns-only 888, rewards-only 331, and no-feedback 12. These are pilot observations from one model invocation per condition, not a reliable ranking across independent runs.

Exactly what each editor received

All conditions retain the task name and objective, observation/action meanings, episode horizon, network architecture, action bounds, and initial random weights. None receives environment source, MuJoCo XML, prior policies, earlier results, or SAC weights. Existing pretrained control knowledge remains.

  • Full trajectories: observations, actions, rewards, next observations, termination/truncation flags, and completed-episode returns.
  • Rewards only: an ordered vector of 4,096 step rewards, without reset markers, observations, actions, episode lengths, or separately computed returns.
  • Returns only: one scalar per completed episode; the final partial episode is excluded. List length inherently reveals the number of completed episodes.
  • No feedback: no environment rollouts before commitment and no rewards, returns, trajectories, or rankings supplied to the editor.

Full/rewards/returns each use 36,864 feedback transitions: one initial-policy block and eight candidate blocks of 4,096. No-feedback uses zero feedback transitions; its 36,864 diagnostic transitions occur only after all twelve editors commit. Held-out evaluation is counted separately. Synthetic network probes use only editor-supplied vectors and provide no environment labels.

All conditions permit complete actor rewrites within the fixed network, without gradients, supervised fitting, or automated parameter search. An editor can resubmit an earlier policy as candidate 8 using its permitted information. The parent never selects by hidden scores.

Candidate histories

Dashed no-feedback curves were measured only after commitment. The editor never saw these scores, and they did not influence selection. Repeated submissions remain visible and consume candidate slots. All 96 submissions were valid.

Survival versus forward movement

Hopper's feedback-enabled policies mostly stand. On Walker2d, full feedback produces slow forward motion and long survival; returns-only nearly stands. Rewards-only moves faster in development but survives about 199 steps on held-out episodes. Return improvements include a substantial survival/stability component.

What this establishes

Pendulum alone is weak evidence that collected experience is necessary: Astra can construct a working controller from prior knowledge. Feedback helps the MuJoCo policies in this pilot, and full trajectories help Walker2d most. Replication across independent editor calls and initialization seeds is needed before attributing a general advantage to a feedback type.

The original study below supplied extra physics/source information, used a different stopping and selection rule, and tested different resets. It is historical context; the fresh full-trajectory condition above is the control for this ablation. Editor file access was restricted by instructions in a shared workspace, not an OS security boundary. Payload whitelists and initial-weight hashes were audited for all 12 cases. Model token and cost telemetry is unavailable.

Original pilot: Astra vs SAC with rich physics context

What the original pilot shows. A reasoning model can construct useful controllers directly inside a randomly initialized neural network. Walker2d is the strongest result; Pendulum is effectively tied, and Hopper mainly stands. This is a feasibility result with substantial physics knowledge, not evidence that weight editing generally outperforms reinforcement learning.

Held-out performance

Higher return is better. Astra and SAC received exactly the same random actor tensors, verified by SHA-256 fingerprints. Astra then directly assigned weights without gradients; SAC trained normally on GPU. No trained policy checkpoint was supplied to Astra.

Training and development curves

The top panels show SAC's exploratory training returns, including a trailing mean over 10 episodes. The bottom panels show Astra's deterministic candidate feedback and the best controller available after each feedback block. Candidate 0 is the initial random policy; every unsuccessful candidate remains visible. These traces use different feedback protocols and are not matched held-out learning curves.

Astra consumed 4,096 initial-policy transitions plus 4,096 per candidate, including partial episodes. It stopped after two candidates on Pendulum and eight on each MuJoCo task. SAC trained to 36,864 steps on all tasks; the Pendulum comparison uses only its saved 12,288-step checkpoint. The gray region shows later SAC training excluded from that matched comparison.

What the policies do

  • Pendulum: an energy-shaping controller plus upright proportional/derivative control. The held-out difference from SAC is −1.80, with a paired interval that includes zero.
  • Hopper: mostly static standing, without sustained hopping. Astra survives all 1,000 steps on every test episode; SAC averages 333.16 steps. Healthy-survival reward explains much of Astra's return.
  • Walker2d: slow alternating/shuffling forward motion, about 0.42 m/s in development. Astra survives all 1,000 steps on every test episode; SAC averages 378.07. The speed is a development observation, not a separately measured held-out speed metric.

Protocol and interpretation

The actor is CleanRL SAC's native network: two 256-unit ReLU layers, mean and log-standard-deviation heads, tanh squashing, and fixed action bounds. All selected Astra candidates replace every actor parameter with explicitly designed control circuits. The architecture and environment remain fixed.

Astra received raw trajectories, observation/action semantics, and native environment Python. The Hopper and Walker2d model XMLs were also supplied on request. Physics and classical-control knowledge supplied the designs; feedback informed sign corrections and other numerical design choices. No gradients, regression, fitting, or automated parameter-search algorithm was used in the Astra arm.

A fresh gpt-6-astra context worked sequentially through Pendulum, Hopper, and Walker2d. Knowledge could transfer within that sequence. Candidate selection used complete-episode mean development return, with the initial random policy also eligible. Only after editing froze did the parent evaluate the selected policies on 100 shared test resets, seeds 41000 through 41099.

SAC used the native CleanRL settings, including 5,000 warmup transitions, and ran on RTX 6000 Ada GPUs. It was neither tuned nor converged at these short budgets. The comparison matches initial actors and online interaction counts, not compute or prior knowledge.

SAC wall times at the matched checkpoints were 52, 223, and 160 seconds. Astra model inference time and billing are unavailable through the runner. Candidate evaluation time excludes reasoning and cannot support a speedup claim. This original-pilot section preserves the original measurements.

Next experiments

  1. Record quantitative dynamics and intervention predictions before editor feedback, then measure error, uncertainty calibration, and transfer under hidden dynamics changes.
  2. Replicate the four feedback conditions across at least five initialization/training seeds and independent editor contexts, prioritizing Walker2d's observed separation. Report forward speed, survival, and control cost alongside return.
  3. Compare with classical-controller and bounded numerical-search baselines, and vary static physics information separately from environment feedback.
  4. Test hidden dynamics perturbations, then whether weight programming accelerates subsequent SAC, counting all editor feedback in the total interaction budget.
